The DPDP Act does not mention AI hiring tools. That does not mean they are unregulated.

The Act has no AI chapter. But its general duties apply. The key one: data used to make a decision about a person must be complete, accurate and consistent.

If an AI screening tool rejects a candidate because it misread a CV, that duty is involved. Security, vendor contracts and data stored abroad also apply.

Simple steps:

• List every AI feature in your ATS and HRMS

• A person reviews AI-based rejections and ratings

• Ask vendors where data is stored and whether it trains their models

• Tell candidates when AI is used (good practice, not a clear legal requirement)

Do you know which of your HR tools use AI today?

“Free” AI training arrives at Indiana community colleges this week under the Mark Cuban Foundation banner, but the press release skips what these programs actually cost to run or to sustain when the pilot fanfare fades.

Ivy Tech’s five-day Agentic AI Academy promises to put AI agents in the hands of non-technical learners, especially in the trades and those returning to the workforce. The curriculum even pulls in a contract-scanning AI from Lift Our Voices to help people spot forced arbitration and NDAs. Participants get a hands-on taste and, by the end, their own “AI agents” to use back on the job.

What’s left unsaid is who pays once the grant winds down. Will these build-your-own-agent tools be free next semester? Or will colleges layering in AI actually find themselves on the hook for more licenses, more support, more integration cleanup, costs that don’t always show up in the pilot’s press cycle, but routinely break the P&L in year two.

Community colleges are built for stretch, not scale. Promising that adults can DIY their way into workplace AI, when the real cost is ongoing platform fees and human patchwork, keeps repeating the same cycle: the demo is subsidized, the rollout eats your margin, and the human support hours only go up. I’m happy to see worker advocacy in the mix, but I’ve watched AI pilots that looked free turn out pricier than hiring another pair of hands.

This was today's top story. I pull the last two weeks of AI news into one running list, always current, here: https://lnkd.in/eSji3KJa

Day 28/100 | How to Beat Payer AI Denials
(Without hiring more billers)

Payer AI can review and deny a claim in seconds. 

If your team is still manually appealing one claim at a time that’s not an efficiency gap it’s a structural disadvantage.

By the time your biller opens the denial, the timely filing clock is already running. 

The claim wasn't wrong. The appeal was just too slow to matter.

Here is how to fix it:
Move the defense upstream: 

Don't wait for the denial.

Re-verify eligibility 48 hours before the visit and check documentation against the code before submission.

Build a priority system:

Stop working denials "easiest first."

Work them by deadline first, then dollar amount.

Put AI and RPA on your side:

Let RPA draft the appeals. Keep 1 human to review and approve. Machine speed, human accuracy.

Know your state laws: Some states now require human review before an AI-driven denial. Cite the statute in your appeal.

Fix the contract:
Add language requiring notice and a seat at the table when payer policy changes hit your revenue.

You don't beat payer AI by working harder by hand. You beat it by moving the check to where it can still save the claim.

Question for practice owners.
When a payer denies a claim today, who owns the appeal a person with a deadline a spreadsheet, or just hope?

An AI agent deleted a company’s entire production database. 

In 9 seconds. 
Backups included. 
Now guess who’s liable.

This is not a horror story from a lab. This happened in April to a real SaaS company, PocketOS: 30+ hours of outage for their customers. The agent wasn’t hacked. It found a token it shouldn't  have seen and did something awesome - it decided to “fix” something, and did. 

And when you look at who pays, it gets worse. 

One analysis found 88% of AI vendors cap their own liability, often at one month of subscription fees. Meanwhile regulators are going the other way: the UK’s CMA says you’re fully responsible for what your agents do, even if someone else built them. California already took away the “the AI did it” defense. The EU is about to treat AI software like any other defective product.

Read that again: Your vendor capped it. Your partner built it. You own it. 

That’s the liability sandwich nobody put in the contracts. And it’s exactly why last week’s “your next partner is an agent” isn’t a utopia. It’s a contract problem. Every agent in that marketplace, every agent your citizen builders fire up, every agent a partner drops into a customer’s system: someone has to answer for it when it goes sideways on an idle Saturday morning at 2 a.m.

So here’s my - mabye a bit provocative - statement: 

the next tiers in partnering won’t be Gold or Platinum. It’ll be Accountability and Experience.

Partners who scope agent permissions, keep audit trails, separate backups and are willing to put their name (and their insurance) behind what they ship will win the deals. The rest will get vetted out by procurement. That's why there will be a lot of focus on well trained and experienced FDEs, governance systems in place, security guardrails properly set up and experience. Here's some bad news: no, you can't train experience! Experience comes with ...well, experiene, i.e. TIME!! So, to all #hiring companies - some of you learned the hard way that replacing seasoned, expensive sellers cannot easily be replaced by way cheaper you sellers (you get awesome pipeline - but little execution) - the same accounts for all roles. There's an argument to be made that experience will cost ya! Don't come back complaining you weren't warned.

Workplace health programmes can reach women who would never pay for care themselves. That is exactly why the guardrails matter.
More employers and insurers are funding women’s health, and I think that is good news. Menopause, fertility and hormonal health have been ignored at work for decades.

But when the person who pays and the person whose body generates the data are not the same person, good intentions are not enough. The design has to protect her.

A few things I keep coming back to:
🔹 Consent at work is never quite free. When a programme runs through your employer, opting out can feel visible. Voluntary on paper is not always voluntary in practice.
🔹 “Aggregate” can still be personal. Workforce-level reports are common, but in a small team, “anonymised women aged 45–55” can mean two or three people. A published minimum group size should be standard.
🔹 Reproductive data deserves its own rules. Menstrual, fertility and menopause data is among the most sensitive data there is. Even aggregated trends should not be able to shape hiring, promotion or pricing decisions.
🔹 “Anonymised forever” is a big promise. Rich wearable and hormonal data is hard to truly anonymise. How long it is kept, and what it is used for, should be clear to her, not just to the buyer.
🔹 Her protections shouldn’t depend on a contract she never sees. And her data should not stay behind when she changes jobs.

The best programmes I have seen get this right. The standard should be that they all do.
If you are buying, brokering or building in this space, ask:
✅ What is the minimum group size for any report?
✅ Is using this data for pricing or underwriting banned in contract?
✅ What happens to her data when she leaves?
✅ Who reviews what the AI tells her, and is that real clinical oversight?

UK job ads asking for cyber security skills more than doubled in a year: 6,487 permanent roles, up from 2,960.

Contract demand grew too: 2,821 contract ads, up from 1,650, at a median of £550 a day.

Where does security sit in your next programme: inside the delivery team, or reviewing it afterwards?

A rating compresses varied experiences into one number. That makes it convenient, but it removes context about scope, expectations and relevance. Two providers with similar scores may have very different strengths. Reading the details helps you understand what customers valued and whether those experiences resemble the work you need.

A review that mentions prompt feedback handling can be valuable when your project involves several stakeholders. A high score without that context tells you less about the specific process you need. Look for patterns relevant to your priorities.

1. Look for repeated patterns across reviews.
2. Read the project context where it is available.
3. Compare those patterns with your priorities.
4. Ask follow-up questions about anything the score cannot explain.

Treat the number as an entry point to evaluation. A sound decision combines the rating with evidence, fit and an understandable delivery plan.
